data.title: Asia stocks choppy after Nvidia earnings as Anthropic pricing looms
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Stocks erased early gains in Asia on Nov 18 after Nvidia posted a better-than-expected sales forecast, as investor confidence remained fragile over questions about the company’s future leadership and potential impacts on its regional supply chain.

In choppy trade, MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan reversed an initial rally to be down 0.1%, narrowly extending its losing streak into a fifth day.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 slid 0.3%, while US S&P 500 e-mini futures clung to gains, up 0.3%.

Despite Nvidia’s upbeat earnings, strategists noted that deeper concerns over the sustainability of AI capital expenditure remain.

Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Bank in Singapore, said: “Nvidia’s results were reassuring and gave investors a reason to refocus on earnings, but they haven’t resolved the broader questions around AI spending returns, financing sustainability and leadership uncertainty.

“So we are seeing an initial relief rally, but not necessarily the conviction needed for a sustained recovery.”

In oil markets, Brent crude futures were 0.6% lower at US$92.60 a barrel in Asian trade, following data showing an increase in US crude and fuel inventories last week.

The ongoing Middle East conflict and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, however, limited losses.

Referendum on AI

Nvidia shares slid 0.5% in after-hours trading, after rising as much as 3.8% following the chipmaker’s third-quarter revenue report and a fourth-quarter forecast that beat market expectations.

The tech company’s earnings report was its first since Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure as chief executive officer in November.

The Wall Street Journal reported that the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is probing Nvidia, citing sources familiar with the matter. The SEC has declined to comment on the matter.

“We’re at a point of peak uncertainty because investors still don’t know what Nvidia’s long-term leadership will look like,” said Brian Colello, senior equity analyst at Morningstar.

Overnight, stocks on Wall Street sold off again, with the S&P 500 down 1% to log a fourth consecutive session lower prior to Nvidia’s earnings report.

“Risk sentiment remained firmly on the defensive overnight, with the tech-led sell-off extending across global markets,” Westpac analysts said in a note.

“I’ve looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI,” said Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion in New York.

“Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies.”

Overnight, stocks on Wall Street sold off again, with the S&P 500 down 1% to log a fourth consecutive session lower prior to Nvidia’s earnings report.

The next health check on the AI industry will come as Anthropic prepares to price its shares later on Nov 18 ahead of its market debut, which could value the company at as much as US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion).

The company has guided its initial public offering price to the top of its range or above, Bloomberg News reported.

“Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies.”

The yen fluctuated between gains and losses, to trade flat against the US dollar at 159.41 yen.

Data showed Japan’s exports rose for a 14th successive month in October, driven by demand for shipments related to semiconductors.

The US dollar index, which measures the greenback’s strength against a basket of six currencies, was steady at 103.60, after reaching its highest level on Nov 17 since April 2, 2025, the date of US President Donald Trump’s Liberation Day tariff announcement.

The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was down 2.1 basis points at 5.08%.

On Nov 17, Alberto Musalem, the St. Louis Fed president who is a non-voter on interest rates in 2026, said that the Federal Reserve may need several rate hikes to bring inflation under control and should act soon to ensure the problem does not get worse.

In cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin was up 0.1% at US$64,347.95, while ether was down 0.1% at US$1,804.06. REUTERS

data.title: Banks pause US$480 million chip loan tied to China’s ByteDance
data.description:
Bankers have frozen work on a US$480 million (S$618 million) loan that would have funded advanced Nvidia chips for use by Chinese technology giant ByteDance, according to sources familiar with the matter.

After the US placed its latest curbs on access to AI chips, bankers at five lenders evaluating the deal have had internal discussions about pulling out or not joining the loan amid fears of violating the new restrictions, the sources said.

Singapore-based neocloud Aolani Cloud recently began inviting banks to join the loan, which would fund the purchase of GPUs (graphics processing units) for a data centre in Malaysia.

But on Nov 16, the US announced a rule requiring data centre operators in countries including Singapore and Malaysia to get a licence to buy advanced AI chips.

The step is aimed at curbing Chinese companies’ remote access to such technology, which is how TikTok parent ByteDance would use the Nvidia GPUs. 

The pause in work on the loan illustrates how the Trump administration’s surprise move has caught many dealmakers in Asia off guard.

Across the region, lenders scrambled on Nov 17 to work out what the new regulations would mean for billions of AI debt in the pipeline and deals that have already been done. 

“We have spent significant time with our banking and financing partners to assess and anticipate regulatory risk ahead of this recent new ruling,” a spokesperson for Aolani said in response to questions about the loan being paused.

“We are proactively working with regulators and our financing partners to ensure the project delivery goes ahead in full compliance with the new ruling.”

DBS Group, which is the mandated lead arranger and book-runner on the deal, declined to comment.

It is not yet clear how exactly the licence approval process will work, and which firms will be required to apply for them. That has prompted a barrage of questions from potential lenders, one of the sources said.

It is unlikely that there will be progress on funding the Aolani deal until bankers can fully evaluate the new rule, the sources said.

Internally, some bankers have described the facility as dead given the risks banks could incur if it was found to violate the new US rule, they said. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Jensen Huang wants job back, as Nvidia to reveal first earnings since scandal
data.description:
WASHINGTON – Former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang said on Nov 17 he wanted his job back, despite resigning over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, marking a new twist for the turmoil-hit AI chip giant hours before it releases a key earnings report.

Investors will scrutinise the results for indications that the artificial intelligence boom can withstand the Nvidia crisis, which highlighted a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies.

Huang, a leading promoter of AI, stepped down last week following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The upheaval has battered shares of Nvidia – until recently the world’s most valuable publicly traded company – which is at the centre of an AI boom that has helped propel markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the globe.

Nvidia has lost US$700 billion (S$902 billion) in market value since the scandal broke, and Huang is to be questioned by US lawmakers on Dec 1 over national security concerns.

But his fall triggered immediate calls from Elon Musk and other entrepreneurs for his return, and even President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang back at Nvidia, downplaying the spy allegations.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said, in his first statement since his resignation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Trump-Xi talks

As the scandal deepened, Washington on Nov 16 announced new restrictions on AI chip exports, drawing condemnation from Beijing.

The new US export curbs and the wider Nvidia scandal risk casting a shadow over talks between Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which starts this week in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US licence to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.

The rules also require licences to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries the US Commerce Department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips.

The changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in South-east Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China.

While the loophole has been known to the authorities, the revelation of Huang’s affair has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice.

His lover Alice Huang, who is not related to the 63-year-old, is a former executive of Megaspeed – a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls.

Business as usual?

Nvidia’s Nov 17 third-quarter results, which are scheduled for 5pm ET (6am on Nov 18 in Singapore), will be the first presented under Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, who is serving as interim CEO.

“If they try to keep a business-as-usual tone in the call, I think that it probably wouldn’t be well received,” said Jacob Bourne of Emarketer.

Investors will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies.

Analysts said they would also be eyeing Nvidia’s guidance on future sales, along with its chip sales in Asia, particularly Singapore.

That could ripple across the AI investments propping up the US economy – with Nvidia backing major labs including Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Nov 19.

Huang on Nov 17 sounded a note of contrition in his statement, saying “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life.” AFP

data.title: Nasdaq-listed HomesToLife lands SGX dual-listing amid rising global demand for custom furniture
data.description:
SINGAPORE – When it comes to furniture shopping, online e-commerce platforms such as Taobao are hugely popular for their easy access to a wide range of mass-market products at affordable prices.

But increasingly, home owners who have more particular tastes are on the hunt for premium-quality furniture that can also be customised to their needs, and local company HomesToLife is bullish that this demand will continue to grow as it secured its secondary listing on the Singapore Exchange.

The Nasdaq-listed company completed a placement of 7.5 million shares on the SGX Mainboard on Nov 17 at $1.15 per share, raising some $8.6 million in gross proceeds. The placement attracted more than 50 accredited and institutional investors, including funds under the Equity Market Development Programme.

Institutional investors, including Amova Asset Management Asia and Lion Global Investors, collectively subscribed for about 4.6 million shares worth around $5.3 million.

UOB Kay Hian acted as the placement agent, while Maybank Securities was the sub-placement agent.

This is the second company to achieve a dual listing on the SGX and Nasdaq, with the first being cybersecurity firm Avepoint in September 2025.

The counter closed flat at $1.15.

About 80% of the $7 million in net proceeds will be used for business expansion, and 20% will be reserved for general working capital.

Chief executive Phua Mei Ming told The Straits Times that the company is seeking to expand its presence in the Asia-Pacific, where it already has a sizeable presence but still has room to grow its distribution.

A burgeoning middle class in markets such as South Korea, Taiwan and Thailand presents good opportunities for HomesToLife’s business, she said.

“We see huge potential in growing not just our premium offering but also a mid-price range of products, as the emerging middle class appreciates well-made products.”

HomesToLife was started by Phua’s father and his two brothers in 1976 as Hwa Tat Lee, one of Singapore’s first sofa makers, with local retailer Courts as one of its major clients. By 1994, it had started its own leather tannery operations here.

In 2014, the current iteration of the brand was launched as a retail business, with six stores in Singapore at its peak. Today, it operates four stores here, with three more in South Korea.

In addition to HomesToLife’s range, the company also owns German luxury brand Domicil, which it acquired in 2005.

Phua said retail comprises only a small percentage of HomesToLife’s business as 95% of its revenue comes from its export business.

Its furniture is sold by major leading retailers around the world, including DFS in the UK and Cuir Center in France.

For its 2025 financial year ended Dec 31, Europe accounted for almost 60% of its revenue at $377.9 million, while 26.9% stemmed from Asia-Pacific, and the rest from North America.

HomesToLife reported $19.4 million in operating profit for FY2025, a 103.7% increase from the previous year. But it also faced cost pressures due to disruptions in the Suez Canal, which raised freight rates by 22%.

Most of the company’s products are made to order, allowing both retail customers and retailers to customise their furniture before they are shipped from factories in China, Vietnam and India.

A number of retailers also carry the brand’s white-labelled products, which are developed and designed exclusively for the retailers’ territories.

Phua said the company is one of the few furniture brands that controls its own supply chain end to end, from design all the way to distribution, where the company would deliver its products to retailers’ warehouses, while other customers may pick them up directly from the port.

The advantage of HomesToLife’s made-to-order model is lower inventory risk for its distributors – if demand for a particular product has waned, for instance, they can flexibly move on to selling new products.

“This is what we call our ‘easy buy, easy sell’ approach to business. We just make it easy for our partners to do their business, which is selling furniture,” she said.

Long-term relationships with most of its retailers, some as long as over 30 years, have also ensured stability in the business. The company has already rented showrooms in a few markets such as Australia and the UK, not for its retail business, but to showcase its products to their local partners.

“These are steps we are taking to ensure that we are the first port of call when customers want to get new ideas on products,” Phua said.

She has observed higher demand for mid-tier and luxury furniture in countries such as South Korea and Japan in spite of weakening economic conditions. For instance, customers in Japan are more likely to pay a higher price for the company’s products because domestic production is unavailable and furniture delivery from Europe takes far too long.

Shrinking domestic furniture production globally due to higher wages and costs of raw materials from China, especially in markets reliant on imports, presents HomesToLife with new opportunities for growth.

Amid competition from online retailers such as Taobao that sell furniture at a fraction of HomesToLife’s prices as they sell direct from the factories, the company does not target the mass market. Rather, Phua said, its own retail outlets’ unique proposition is the ability to guarantee customers that they are getting the most value through its quality assurance.

“Our strengths lie in customisation and comfort, and at the retail level we are targeting the consumer who wants the full suite of service – from helping them to take measurements to confirming their purchase is the right size and comfort level, and then organising their delivery.”

She added that there are few competitors that have the same scale as HomesToLife when it comes to its “unrivalled” range of offerings. For instance, the company has 20 different types of fabric and 10 leather options. It is also one of the leading companies in embedding technology such as dual-motor reclining systems, speakers and even Bluetooth-synced vibration in its sofas to deliver a 4D home cinema experience.

“There is very low customer churn because of the way we service and support our customers,” Phua said, referring to its retail partners. “You might need a few different players to replace us.”

Its parent company, HTL International, was delisted from the SGX in 2016 and acquired by Chinese furniture company Yihua Lifestyle Technology. It was placed under judicial management in 2020 as the Covid-19 pandemic crippled its manufacturing business.

In 2021, an entity beneficially owned by the founding Phua brothers acquired the company out of judicial management, and HomesToLife listed on Wall Street in 2024 to access the capital markets there for expanding its business.

The company’s share price has fallen over 250% from its initial public offering price of US$4 to US$1.13 on Nov 16.

Phua acknowledged the challenge of attracting investors on a bourse dominated by tech companies, which is one of the reasons why it has chosen to list on the SGX as well.

She also cited recent initiatives to rejuvenate the local stock market, as well as to support the growth of Singapore companies, as a major consideration for HomesToLife’s dual listing.

“A homecoming to SGX makes sense for us as a home-grown company to increase awareness among the investing public. Listing here would also give us the credibility to expand in the region.”

data.title: Disney beats earnings forecasts, plans to increase content spending
data.description:
LOS ANGELES – Walt Disney on Nov 17 reported quarterly revenue and earnings that beat Wall Street expectations, helped by higher theme park attendance and strong NFL viewership, and said it would increase content spending by 9% in the next fiscal year.

Disney reported adjusted earnings per share of US$1.77 for the fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct 3. Analysts had forecast US$1.67 on average, according to LSEG.

The owner of the Disney+ streaming service and ESPN cable network said it would boost cash content spending to US$26 billion (S$33.5 billion) in 2027, including by investing more in international programming and sports rights.

The company plans to cut operating expenses by about US$3 billion by fiscal 2029, executives said in a letter to shareholders.

Shares of Disney, however, dipped nearly 2% in premarket trading. The company’s projection for total full-year operating income growth of 8% was lower than the 12% increase reported in the just-ended fiscal year.

New chief executive Josh D’Amaro, who took charge at Disney in March, is steering the company through a consumer shift to streaming and competition from social media platforms such as YouTube and TikTok.

D’Amaro has said he wants to strengthen Disney’s streaming business and continue to invest in theme parks and cruise lines.

Disney said it saw increased engagement in the reported quarter across its streaming platforms and that it was also investing in short-form programming and creator-driven content to boost engagement. Subscription Video on Demand, or SVOD, revenue jumped 19% to US$6.1 billion.

At the entertainment division, which includes streaming, ABC and other networks, revenue rose 17% to US$11.9 billion, helped by higher subscription revenue. Operating income at the segment rose 92% to US$1.3 billion.

The company, however, said it would stop disclosing SVOD operating income, adding that it no longer believes the metric “reflects this segment focus and strategy”.

Total revenue rose 16% to US$25.9 billion in the latest quarter, topping estimates. The company also said its board agreed to raise the annual shareholder dividend by 33% to US$2 per share, paid in US$1 installments in January and July.

The experiences division, home to theme parks and cruise ships, reported record revenue and profit. The unit’s revenue rose 15% to US$10.1 billion and operating income increased 20% to nearly US$2.3 billion.

At sports, revenue rose 16% to US$4.6 billion as ESPN viewership for the start of the NFL and college football seasons reached record highs. The segment’s operating income increased by 53% to nearly US$1.4 billion.

Looking ahead, Disney reiterated that it expected double-digit growth in adjusted earnings per share in fiscal 2027.

It said total segment operating income would grow about 8% for the year. The company plans capital expenditures of about US$9 billion, similar to the current fiscal year. REUTERS

data.title: Wall Street ends mixed after Nvidia earnings, Fed minutes
data.description:
NEW YORK - US stocks were mixed on Nov 18 as investors digested Nvidia results ahead of Anthropic’s initial public offering pricing, while weighing hawkish sentiment reflected in US Federal Reserve minutes.

After gyrating early in the session, the Nasdaq closed modestly higher, the Dow ended sharply lower, while the S&P 500 reversed its modest gains to settle in negative territory following the Fed minutes release.

Nvidia’s quarterly results released late on Nov 17 beat analyst expectations, and the AI chipmaker forecast quarterly revenue above estimates. Even so, its shares fell amid uncertainties caused by co-founder Jensen Huang’s sudden departure last week.

The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index, which has handily outperformed the broader market this year, closed slightly lower, underscoring lofty expectations for the sector amid massive spending on AI infrastructure and potential risk associated with the nascent technology.

Anthropic’s IPO is expected to price after the market closes on Nov 18. At the top of its US$70 to US$78 range, the offering would raise about US$64.4 billion and value the company at about US$1.4 trillion.

Other chipmakers were mixed. Intel and Micron lost ground, but Advanced Micro Devices advanced.

“There’s been a lot of dark clouds of uncertainty over technology, chip stocks and AI in general,” said Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group in Omaha.

“It’s important to remember the market’s not totally falling apart here. It clearly is top-heavy with tech, but there are other groups that are actually doing pretty well under the surface.”

Target jumped following the discount retailer’s upbeat holiday outlook. Results from its larger rival Walmart are expected on Nov 19.

TJX surged after forecasting upbeat annual sales, banking on strong demand ahead of the holiday shopping season.

Take-Two Interactive shares rose ahead of the rollout of its Grand Theft Auto VI video game.

According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 18 points, or 0.24%, to end at 7,322.53 points, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 101.50 points, or 0.39%, to 24,429.89.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 566.39 points, or 1.12%, to 50,193.03.

Focus on the US Fed

Minutes from the Fed’s October policy meeting showed the central bank remained focused on inflation risks, recognising the need for further rate hikes if the economy progresses as expected. A few policymakers argued the case for a 50-basis-point rate hike “if incoming inflation data were unfavourable.”

Consumer and producer price data released after the October meeting showed hotter-than-expected price growth.

Fed governor Christopher Waller took a hawkish stance on Nov 18, saying the central bank needs to be more aggressive in responding to inflation. This follows John Williams’ comments on Nov 17, in which the New York Fed president said that while he favours tighter monetary policy, there was no need for “dramatic action.”

Financial markets are pricing in a near-certain probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike at the conclusion of the Fed’s December meeting, according to CME’s FedWatch tool.

“Inflation continues to be stubbornly higher than anyone wants,” Detrick said. “The Fed’s going to probably do a 25-basis-point hike in December, and a couple more hikes early next year is a very real possibility.”

Housing data released on Nov 18 showed mortgage rates climbing, building permits faltering, and pending home sales dropping to a record low. REUTERS

data.title: ‘Almost all’ US Fed policymakers saw further interest rate hikes as likely, minutes show
data.description:
WASHINGTON - “Almost all” participants of the US Federal Reserve’s interest rate-setting meeting in October thought that further rate hikes would be necessary to fight stubbornly high inflation, minutes of the meeting showed on Nov 18.

The meeting’s minutes, released after a customary three-week lag, showed that according to almost all policymakers’ baseline outlooks for inflation and the labour market, further rate hikes “would likely be appropriate” to bring prices back under control.

The US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady at its last meeting in late October, even as its chairman, Kevin Warsh, said inflation remained “too high.”

The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75 and 4%, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.

Two voting members, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, had dissented in favour of an immediate 25-basis-point hike.

‘Broad-based’ inflation

The Fed has a dual mandate of keeping inflation to its long-term 2% target while ensuring maximum employment.

The unemployment rate in the United States has been relatively steady over the last year, even as job growth has seesawed. That stability is due to demographic changes and lower immigration.

Inflation, on a downward trajectory since hitting a pandemic peak, has reignited in the last year, driven by US President Donald Trump’s tariff policies and the energy price spike caused by his war on Iran.

The massive investments in infrastructure to support the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout have also led to increased prices.

Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index inflation, the Fed’s preferred gauge, hit 3.6% in September, far above the central bank’s target.

At the meeting in October, participants “acknowledged that inflation remained elevated.”

“Most remarked that inflation pressures in the economy were broad-based,” indicating they saw price increases as having spread beyond skyrocketing energy prices into other sectors.

Still, 10 of the committee’s 12 voting members called for rates to be held steady.

“These participants cited the need to assess the durability of AI-related investment demand, the evolution of financing conditions, the transmission of the September rate increase to the economy, or geopolitical developments,” the minutes said.

Those who dissented from the majority decision in calling for a 25-basis-point hike said they saw inflation as “too high” and “saw few signs of it abating.”

“They judged that the current policy stance was not sufficiently restrictive, and a few of them warned that further delay risked allowing high inflation to become entrenched or necessitating a larger and more disruptive tightening later.”

‘Concerned’

Speaking to US broadcaster CNBC on the morning of Nov 18, before the minutes were released, Fed governor Chris Waller said he was “very, very concerned” about inflation and now saw the need for a 50-basis-point hike at the Fed’s next meeting in December.

“If you really want to get it down, you’ve got to start taking more aggressive actions,” he said.

He said the Fed may need to go beyond the December rate hike he prescribed in order to meaningfully fight inflation.

Fed governor Michael Barr, speaking at an event in New York on Nov 18, also said he saw the need for further rate hikes. AFP

data.title: Troubled Australian retailer David Jones to cut 1,500 jobs, union says
data.description:
SYDNEY – Troubled Australian department store chain David Jones will cut about 1,500 jobs across 19 stores slated for closure following its collapse into administration, a union said on Nov 18.

The Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association said only 170 of the 1,689 impacted store workers had been offered redeployment opportunities.

David Jones entered administration on Nov 5, with directors citing difficult trading conditions, online competition and weak household spending as reasons for its failure.

At the first meeting of creditors on Nov 17, administrators McGrathNicol said the retailer owed at least A$459 million (S$398 million) to an array of creditors, including A$11 million to 6,242 employees.

“We are very disappointed that of the 1,689 jobs of directly employed David Jones workers at risk in the 19 stores set to close, the company is offering only 170 job redeployments, barely one in 10,” said Bernie Smith, secretary of the union’s New South Wales state branch.

“This is a missed opportunity both for the workers and for the business to reset the service level they could provide that David Jones was once known for.”

The union was continuing to work to secure members’ unpaid entitlements, Smith added.

FTI Consulting, the appointed receivers, declined to comment when asked about the job losses.

It has said it plans to close 18 of David Jones’ 37 stores across Australia and one in New Zealand by the end of the year.

A sale process is also under way, with administrators saying on Nov 17 they had contacted 150 potential buyers, local and international.

Founded in Sydney in 1838 by Welsh immigrant David Jones, the retailer describes itself as the world’s oldest continuously operating department store.

Australian private equity firm Anchorage Capital Partners acquired the chain in 2023 with plans to turn the business around, yet losses continued as rent and employee costs rose.

It entered administration after landlords did not agree to rent concessions and a plan to restructure the store network. REUTERS

data.title: Wall Street ends lower ahead of Nvidia earnings, Anthropic debut
data.description:
NEW YORK - US stocks extended their tech-driven slide on Nov 17 as investors braced for Nvidia’s earnings, expected just after the bell. Scandal and controversy have surrounded the chip giant in recent days, fuelling worries over the rapid build-out of AI infrastructure and risks associated with the nascent technology.

Those jitters intensified ahead of Anthropic’s mammoth IPO, expected on Nov 18, which is targeted to raise as much as US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion).

All three major US stock indexes closed sharply lower.

The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq notched their first four-day streak of declines since September.

“Every sector in the S&P is down,” said Oliver Pursche, senior vice-president at Wealthspire Advisors, in New York. “So clearly, it is a reflection of overall investor nervousness as opposed to being driven by a specific set of stocks, whether they’re AI-related or not.”

“It’s a confluence of all of the events that are there, and it seems to be speculation-driven as opposed to fact-driven,” Pursche added. “It’s not all about Nvidia.”

The AI trade was already contending with popular opposition to large data centres when tech shares were rocked by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster following revelations of his relationship with an alleged spy. Investors are also impatient to see returns on hyperscalers’ massive expenditures.

The Trump administration’s plans to block imports of Chinese data centre equipment gained momentum in the wake of Huang’s departure, despite opposition from Amazon, Alphabet , Meta and others.

Expectations leading up to Nvidia’s results were sky-high. The company was projected to post 90.4% year-on-year earnings growth on revenue of US$109.11 billion. The stock ended the session in negative territory.

Enthusiasm over artificial intelligence helped send the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index’s year-to-date gain as high as 106% in June, but that fervour has since lost steam. The index’s gains so far this year have shrunk to about 34%.

Economic data released early in the session showed strong underlying retail sales, weakening industrial output and rising import prices, largely driven by spiking petroleum costs. Homebuilder sentiment plunged to its lowest level since April 2012.

According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 75.96 points, or 1.02%, to end at 7,341.23 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 180.42 points, or 0.74%, to 24,329.34.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 859.71 points, or 1.67%, to 50,748.46.

On the sector level, software and services, airlines and banks were clear underperformers.

Intel fell after Nvidia cut its stake in the company by 25%.

Software shares were broadly lower, with Salesforce, Workday, Intuit and Adobe all losing ground.

Microsoft also declined on the day.

JPMorgan shares dipped after the company said insider Bregje de Best would succeed Jeremy Barnum as chief financial officer in early 2027.

Fed hints at aggressive rate hikes

Fed officials are increasingly suggesting that stubborn inflation has made the central bank more open to an aggressive US rate-hike path.

Markets are pricing in a near-certain 95.4% likelihood of a 25-basis-point increase in December, according to CME’s FedWatch tool.

On Nov 18, minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee’s October meeting could help illuminate the central bank’s approach to near-term monetary policy. REUTERS

data.title: US Federal Reserve’s Lisa Cook refuses to participate in White House hearing
data.description:
WASHINGTON – Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear in December before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome.

The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook’s lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration initially demanded for Nov 6.

Trump administration officials have demanded that Cook appear before the committee to address allegations she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed’s board of governors, a charge she denies.

President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president’s efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed’s independence and reflect Trump’s desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs.

“Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing – and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook’s lawyer, wrote in a letter released on Nov 17 to White House counsel William Scharf.

The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a facade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook.”

In June, the Supreme Court blocked the Trump administration from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that “the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design.” AP

data.title: Singlife to phase out Singlife Account insurance savings plan by end-2027
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Home-grown insurer Singlife will discontinue its savings and insurance product Singlife Account, with all remaining accounts to be closed by Dec 16, 2027.

Singlife said it generally does not disclose customer numbers for individual products.

The decision to discontinue Singlife Account is “part of our ongoing review of our product offerings to ensure they remain relevant to customers’ evolving financial needs”, said a Singlife spokesperson on Nov 18.

In an e-mail on Nov 16 at about 5pm, Singlife Account executive director Bernard Low notified customers of the account closure, providing details on what to expect from the changes. Customers also received a pop-up notification on their Singlife app.

Singlife will also stop accepting new account applications.

The closure date depends on the account value. If an account has remained below $100 for more than 120 days as of Nov 11, 2026, it will be closed on Dec 16, 2026. If the 120-day mark is reached after Nov 11, 2026, the account will be closed in the following month.

Accounts with $100 and above will be closed on Dec 16, 2027. Until then, customers with at least $100 in their accounts can continue to make top-ups and withdrawals, earn the base rate of 1.5% per annum, and continue to be covered as long as their policy remains in force.

The insurance coverage bundled with the Singlife Account will lapse when the account is closed, but customers can still submit claims for insured events that occurred while the policy was in force.

From Dec 16, 2026, customers will no longer be able to make payments to third-party merchants using funds from the Singlife Account via PayNow UEN.

Customers can opt to withdraw their funds earlier, but the account will still be closed on its scheduled date. Singlife urged customers to make sure they have linked and updated their bank account details in the Singlife app so that their remaining funds can be returned to them automatically. If the refund process fails, customers will be contacted.

The discontinuation of Singlife Account does not affect customers who hold other insurance policies with Singlife.

Singlife was founded by former HSBC Insurance Singapore CEO Walter de Oude in 2014. He led Singlife’s acquisition of Aviva Singapore in 2020 and their subsequent integration, before leaving the firm. He launched financial services platform Chocolate Finance in 2024.

In several Reddit threads posted on Nov 16, some customers discussed alternatives to switch their cash to, laying out other options in the market, such as MariBank, GXS Bank, Trust Bank, Syfe, Chocolate Finance and SingFinance.

The Singlife Account, launched in 2019, is an insurance savings plan that functions much like a savings account, allowing customers to earn returns on their deposits with no lock-in period and fees. It also provides payment features, and death or terminal illness coverage of up to 105% of the account value.

In a media release announcing Singlife’s merger with Aviva Singapore in 2020, it reported that the Singlife Account hit 100,000 downloads within the first three months of launch, with customers entrusting almost $500 million through the product.

It was also referred to as a “mobile-first” insurance savings plan.

At the time, customers could earn 2.5% interest per annum on their first $10,000 with an initial contribution of $500.

Singlife is now a wholly owned subsidiary of Sumitomo Life, a Japanese insurer based in Osaka.

“Customer needs have evolved, and we are focusing our efforts on developing solutions that better serve our customers,” said the firm’s spokesperson.

As demand for legacy planning solutions grows, the insurer recently introduced newer insurance savings plans, such as Singlife Heritage Income, to help individuals preserve and distribute their wealth.

data.title: UOB to use A*STAR’s multilingual AI tool to guide S-E Asia relationship managers on client calls
data.description:
SINGAPORE – UOB and A*STAR have tied up to explore how an artificial intelligence tool can help relationship managers better engage clients, as the bank drives greater deployment of AI across its operations.

The tool is designed to transcribe and translate customer calls in real time, and prompt relationship managers with questions to ask and disclosures to make so they comply with regulatory guidelines.

Built on A*STAR’s large language model MERaLiON, the AI solution can understand 11 languages and dialects spoken in South-east Asia, where UOB’s retail customers are concentrated.

“(We) see potential for this solution to help our relationship managers better understand customers, navigate language and cultural nuances, and provide clearer, more relevant guidance,” said UOB’s group chief financial officer Leong Yung Chee in a statement on Nov 18 on the first day of the Singapore FinTech Festival.

In a demonstration to the media on Nov 13, UOB and A*STAR showed a mock customer call in which an early version of the tool could log sentences spoken in a mix of English, Mandarin and Malay.

When the relationship manager neglected to properly verify the client’s identity, the tool flagged it in red, prompted her to ask for an NRIC number and suggested a scripted line.

Panchai Aroonpairoj, a senior client adviser at UOB Private Bank, said the tool could come in handy when he speaks with older Thai clients, who may sometimes use Teochew phrases during their calls.

As he does not understand the dialect, he would otherwise have to ask them to repeat themselves in Thai, disrupting the flow of the conversation.

UOB believes that the solution could also provide insights for more targeted coaching of relationship managers, complementing existing training methods such as role-playing while a human observer gives feedback.

The bank hopes to roll out the AI tool some time in 2027, though there is no fixed timeline yet, said UOB’s head of enterprise AI Alvin Eng.

For now, A*STAR and UOB will work on developing the application and tailoring it to the bank’s needs.

Angela Chee, a director at A*STAR’s Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing, said this would mark MERaLiON’s first use case in the banking sector.

Other banks such as DBS, OCBC and Standard Chartered have also been testing the model and evaluating how they would use it.

The model’s existing users include social service agency Lions Befrienders, which has a MERaLiON-powered voice agent to automate check-in calls on seniors, and tech service provider NCS, which uses the model for voice transcription for its in-house chatbot.

“A large part of our work will be doing model adaptation to see how we can teach the model to speak or to think like a financial person, so (it) can transcribe more accurately,” said Chee.

A*STAR will have to familiarise MERaLiON with the terminology and acronyms that UOB uses, and incorporate feedback from the bank as it tests the solution.

UOB, like many banks, has been stepping up its deployment of AI to streamline workflows and drive value. It has more than 300 AI and data analytics use cases, including a solution that optimises cash replenishment routes and schedules for its ATMs.

The MERaLiON solution will not supplant its relationship managers. “That’s not our philosophy,” said Eng, adding that the tool is meant to augment staff.

For Aroonpairoj, the value of his team is clear. “You need relationships, which means you need human touch,” he said. “People will trust humans more than machines.”

data.title: Anthropic’s IPO: Will Singapore investors back AI’s promise or help fuel another bubble?
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Anthropic’s upcoming listing will put the market’s appetite for artificial intelligence to the test.

Do investors still see AI as a lucrative opportunity? Or have concerns over lofty valuations, soaring spending and uncertain returns brought them back down to earth?

The Nov 19 Nasdaq listing of the company behind the Claude chatbot comes amid significant volatility in AI-related stocks.

Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion), according to its latest initial public offering (IPO) plans. It is offering 825 million shares at between US$70 and US$78 apiece, potentially raising US$64.4 billion, including shares sold by existing shareholders, which could make it the biggest IPO in history.

A strong debut would signal that investors still see fortunes to be made from AI.

Conversely, a lacklustre one might suggest that investors are becoming more discerning about the prices they are prepared to pay for the stock.

A subsequent fall in Anthropic’s share price could signal either a broader loss of confidence in AI or a reassessment of the company’s valuation and prospects.

This does not have to be a bad thing, though. Given the transformational potential and benefits of AI, a correction could be an opportunity for more sensible, long-term value investors to enter the market.

Promise and peril

Founded in 2021, the San Francisco-based company develops the Claude family of AI models used for tasks ranging from writing and software development to research and data analysis.

Anthropic plans to use the proceeds from the offering and a concurrent US$26 billion private placement to fund general corporate purposes, including investments in computing infrastructure, research and development, and business expansion.

Its prospectus points to the technology’s potential to accelerate scientific discoveries, help researchers tackle diseases such as cancer and improve productivity across both the public and private sectors.

In healthcare, for example, AI could help doctors identify diseases earlier and aid researchers in developing new treatments. In education, it could provide personalised learning support, while businesses could use it to improve efficiency and reduce costs.

The strategic and national importance of AI is also evident in the lengths to which the US has gone to restrict China’s access to advanced semiconductors.

On Nov 16, Washington announced new restrictions requiring US export licences for shipments of certain advanced AI chips to data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, among other countries, as it seeks to prevent Chinese companies from accessing American computing power through overseas facilities.

The rule underscores the urgency with which the Commerce Department is scrambling to crack down on Chinese access to sensitive American technology, following reporting that the agency turned a blind eye to smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China.

But Anthropic’s prospectus also lays bare the formidable costs and risks of developing the technology.

The company further warned that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity if developed or deployed without adequate safeguards.

Such risks could arise if AI systems were weaponised, misused or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy, particularly if advances in the technology outpace developers’ ability to evaluate and control them.

The prospectus also highlights the possibility that increasingly autonomous systems could take harmful actions without human intervention.

Meanwhile, the company is still unprofitable, recording a net loss of US$104 billion for the first nine months of the year, compared with US$25.1 billion in the same period in 2025.

Anthropic has also disclosed approximately US$900.9 billion in purchase and lease commitments, much of it related to computing capacity and infrastructure extending over many years.

These levels of expenditure raise questions about whether the company can sustain its growth, maintain its technological advantage and generate sufficient profits to justify investors’ expectations.

Lessons from past bubbles

But even a strong debut could prompt questions about whether speculation is running ahead of economic reality.

Investors would do well to remember what happened during the dot.com boom.

In the late 1990s, investors poured money into internet companies on the assumption that the new technology would transform commerce and communication.

While they were right about the internet’s potential, many were wrong about the companies they backed and the prices they paid.

The lesson was that investors could correctly anticipate a technological revolution and still lose fortunes betting on it.

The cryptocurrency boom and bust offers another warning.

Cryptocurrencies attracted investors with promises of decentralised finance, better financial infrastructure and attractive returns. But soaring crypto prices also encouraged speculation, excessive leverage and a culture of hype and excess.

The collapse of the TerraUSD stablecoin and its sister token Luna in May 2022 triggered heavy losses and exposed vulnerabilities across the sector.

The crisis deepened in November that year with the implosion of FTX, once one of the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchanges. Founder Sam Bankman-Fried was subsequently convicted of fraud and sentenced to 25 years in prison.

The crypto collapse showed that investor enthusiasm can easily obscure fundamental questions about viability, governance, transparency and risk.

While AI is already generating substantial commercial revenue and delivering practical benefits across industries, the danger is the formation of another speculative bubble.

When expectations eventually disappoint, a sharp market correction could erode confidence across the sector, including companies with sound business models and promising technologies. The result could be a setback for innovation and development of AI, even if the technology’s underlying potential remains intact.

Anthropic’s investors, therefore, face the difficult task of putting a price on a technology that promises benefits, even as its developers acknowledge costs and risks that are difficult to predict and quantify.

What is clear is that greater scrutiny following a Democratic sweep in the US midterms would put pressure on AI companies to exercise financial discipline, rein in excessive spending and demonstrate that their products can generate sustainable profits.

It could encourage investors to pay closer attention to safety and corporate governance, particularly when failures could have far-reaching consequences for society and shareholders.

Nvidia offers a stark reminder of why governance matters.

The chipmaker, whose market value grew more than tenfold from the end of 2022 to its peak in October 2026, became the poster child of the AI boom under co-founder Jensen Huang.

But Huang’s abrupt resignation in November exposed the risks of a company so closely identified with one individual, particularly when it had no publicly known successor ready to take over.

Nvidia has lost about US$1.8 trillion in market value since its October peak, weighed down by concerns over AI valuations compounded by uncertainty over its leadership and future direction.

Its predicament shows that even a company with strong earnings and a commanding market position can suffer when investors begin questioning its governance.

AI may well change the world for the better. But that does not mean investors should pay any price for a stake in its future.

data.title: Citi settles sexual harassment claims by managing director
data.description:
Citigroup has settled a high-profile lawsuit by a managing director who claimed the bank had for years tolerated sexual harassment, assault and gender-based discrimination against her.

Ardith Lindsey sued Citi three years ago, claiming she had been the subject of “prolonged, pervasive and outrageous mistreatment” during her 16 years in the bank’s global equities markets division.

Lindsey had spent her entire Wall Street career at Citi, starting as the most junior member on the electronic sales trading desk, before later taking charge of the desk in 2021, when she was promoted to managing director.

A lawyer for Lindsey, Jeremiah Iadevaia, told the court in a letter on the night of Nov 13 that they had finalised a deal to resolve the case, after months of negotiations.

No terms of the agreement were made public.

The two sides announced in June that they had reached a “settlement in principle” after engaging in mediation. 

Neither Citigroup nor Iadevaia immediately responded to phone messages seeking comment.

“Our values and expectations are clear – no one should ever be discriminated against or harassed in the workplace,” Citigroup said in an earlier statement.

Lindsey, a University of Virginia graduate, joined Citigroup in October 2007.

She alleged that another, more senior Citigroup executive had coerced her into an abusive relationship and threatened her and her family with violence after she ended it in October 2022.

Lindsey’s suit also alleged a sexual assault by a superior when she first started at the bank and claimed there was a “boys’ club” culture at Citigroup’s equities group, including suggestive comments, traders mocking the firm’s sexual harassment policies and frequent outings to strip clubs. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Nvidia chairman says board does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO
data.description:
SANTA CLARA – Nvidia on Nov 17 rejected Jensen Huang’s offer to return as chief executive, putting to rest for now any possible reinstatement of the celebrated artificial intelligence billionaire and industry evangelist, despite pressure from Silicon Valley and support from US President Donald Trump.

The embattled company’s board of directors “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call before yielding to chief financial officer Colette Kress, who is running the company while the board searches for a permanent replacement.

The rejection caps a whirlwind few days triggered by Huang’s admission to extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman and suspected spy for Beijing, his stunning ouster and a surprising split in the Trump administration over the fate of the disgraced business leader.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a wholesale cleaning at Nvidia on Nov 15, only for Trump to come out in support of Huang’s return the next day despite investigations into whether Nvidia had allowed AI chips banned from China to slip through the cracks because of the alleged spy.

Earlier on Nov 17, Huang said in a social media post that if the board decided that his return was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and the country, he would be “honoured to answer these calls”.

Huang acknowledged making “serious mistakes” in his personal life but said that he has received an “outpouring” of support from employees, investors, business partners and customers for his return.

Tech figures, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, have called for Huang's reinstatement, a high-profile booster of the artificial intelligence industry who oversaw Nvidia’s rise as the key provider of chips driving advanced AI models.

Trump, a Huang ally who has spoken with him frequently, has also endorsed the comeback bid.

In its third-quarter earnings statement released on Nov 17, Nvidia did not mention Huang’s ouster or his possible return.

The turmoil notwithstanding, Nvidia blew past Wall Street expectations for the quarter, pulling in around US$116 billion (S$150 billion) in revenue, double the level from a year ago. The company also posted net income of US$2.70 per share, beating estimates of US$2.48 per share.

Nvidia stock shot up 5.2% in after-hours trading.

Referring to Huang’s replacement, Jones said: “We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.”

Petition drive seeks Huang’s return

A “Stand with Jensen” petition set up last week has gathered momentum, gaining signatures from current and former Nvidia staff, investors and other Silicon Valley supporters. It calls on the board to bring back Huang while an independent investigation proceeds or until there’s “compelling evidence” that his departure is in the company’s best interests.

“We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the organisers said in an open letter. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the centre of this controversy was a spy.”

Trump suggested on Nov 16 that the former CEO could return, saying Huang “learnt a big lesson” and that he “would certainly not mind” if he were reinstated.

Huang resigned last week from Nvidia, apparently ousted by the board after revelations that he had extramarital affairs, both with the woman suspected of being a Chinese spy and with a senior executive who reported to him.

The woman reportedly had links to Chinese intelligence was an executive at Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed International, a company being investigated by the US for allegedly violating US export controls by illegally diverting advanced Nvidia AI chips to Chinese companies.

Huang faces questioning by Congress

Also on Nov 17, key House lawmakers said that Huang has voluntarily agreed to appear for transcribed interviews as the company faces intensifying national scrutiny over sales of its advanced computer chips.

Huang will appear before congressional committees on Dec 1, followed by the company’s general counsel, Tim Teter, on Dec 2.

“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” said a statement from the chairmen of three House committees with oversight of China and intelligence issues.

“The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal,” the lawmakers said, referring to the People’s Republic of China.

Meanwhile, Nvidia said it’s creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance following the revelations about Huang.

Nvidia’s advanced chips are in high demand because they are essential for cloud computing and data centres that underpin the AI boom, but they face restrictions on their sale to China. Trump said it was “good” that Nvidia had created the new oversight committee.

“Yes, that’s a good idea. It’s a great company,” Trump said shortly after arriving on Nov 17 in the Philippine capital of Manila, where he took photos with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan. “It’s a great idea.” AP

data.title: Canada’s La Caisse in talks for stake in Bain’s Singapore-based Bridge Data Centres, sources say
data.description:
HONG KONG – Canadian pension fund La Caisse has emerged as the leading bidder in advanced talks for a stake in Bain Capital’s Bridge Data Centres (BDC), two people with knowledge of the matter said.

Bain Capital kicked off a sale process for at least 40% of BDC shares earlier in 2026, targeting a valuation of US$5 billion (S$6.45 billion), which drew interest from private equity, infrastructure and pension funds, Reuters has reported.

The size of the stake La Caisse would buy is still being negotiated, but Bain Capital could be selling up to half of its holdings in the Singapore-based firm, said one of the people.

A deal could be signed in the coming weeks, but the talks with La Caisse are not exclusive and terms not finalised, the person added.

Some bidders were looking at a valuation of US$4 billion for BDC, said a third person with knowledge of the transaction.

Bain Capital, BDC and La Caisse did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. All the people declined to be named due to confidentiality.

BDC operates data centres in Malaysia, Thailand and India, one of many companies that have been aggressively building capacity in Asia over the past two years to meet surging demand for cloud computing, AI and digital services.

TikTok-owner ByteDance was the anchor tenant at the first phase of BDC’s MY06 hyperscale data centre in Johor, Malaysia, according to a BDC release.

But BDC is seeking to diversify its customer base and has signed new contracts with global tech companies, one of the people said.

The talks on the sale of a stake in BDC come at a time when sentiment in the sector has soured on concerns about mounting debt-funded AI spending.

Worsening the outlook, South-east Asia’s US$100 billion-plus AI industry faces fresh US curbs on advanced chip exports to the region, announced on Nov 16, aiming to restrict Chinese companies’ access to computing power to train AI models.

BDC was founded a decade ago by industry veterans Michael Foust and Kris Kumar in partnership with Bain Capital, which merged the firm into Chinese data centre operator Chindata in 2019 and listed the combined business on the Nasdaq in 2020.

The two businesses were separated again under a new entity WinTriX after Bain Capital took Chindata private in 2023 in a US$3.16 billion deal.

In January, Bain Capital completed the sale of Chindata to a consortium led by Shenzhen Dongyangguang Industry that valued the business at US$4 billion. REUTERS

data.title: Brief rally for S’pore tech stocks after Nvidia’s strong earnings exceed forecasts
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Singapore tech stocks opened firmer on Nov 18, following Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings call at 6am Singapore time, quickly pared gains in intra-day trading as weaker sentiment in the tech industry persisted, but ended higher when the market closed.

Shares of AEM Holdings climbed 4% to $6.58 when the market opened, while UMS Integration’s and Frencken Group’s counters rose 2.4% to $1.73 and $1.74 respectively. But by 9.45am, all three stocks had reversed their gains to trade in negative territory, continuing the industry-wide slide that had begun in October as investors became increasingly cautious about the massive AI capital expenditures.

Both AEM and Frencken were trading below the previous day’s close at the mid-day break, while UMS’ counter was flat. At the close, UMS was 3% higher at $1.74, Frencken was up 0.6% at $1.71 and AEM gained 3.5% to end at $6.55.

The brief rally among the Singapore tech stocks suggests investors are willing to acknowledge strong AI fundamentals, but are not yet ready to overlook the broader risks, said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Singapore.

The momentary boost came from Nvidia’s strong earnings for the third quarter ended Oct 25, which exceeded analysts’ expectations.

The US chipmaking giant’s revenue for the quarter more than doubled to US$115.8 billion (S$149.3 billion) from a year ago, beating estimates of US$109.1 billion and marking the 17th straight quarter that it has topped Wall Street’s revenue expectations.

Meanwhile, its net income also rose 105% year on year to US$65.3 billion.

The company expects even higher revenue – about US$130 billion – next quarter and has raised 2027’s growth outlook to about 75%, on the back of strong, broadening AI demand for Vera Rubin, its newest generation of AI processors.

This points to sustained spending across the chip supply chain and supports order books for Singapore’s tech and precision engineering firms, said Ritesh Ganeriwal, managing director and group head of investment and advisory at Syfe.

He noted that these firms are one step removed from the data centres most directly affected by the new US curbs announced on Nov 16, which ensure restrictions on access to sensitive US technology are not circumvented through remote computing arrangements, such as involving data centres in third countries including Singapore.

“Their shares may still swing with sentiment, but their orders depend on global chip investment, which Nvidia’s results show remains strong,” said Ganeriwal. He added that customer concentration and order visibility will differentiate the winners among semiconductor and precision engineering firms which benefit from sustained AI investment in a selective and potentially volatile recovery towards the year-end.

While Nvidia’s earnings were strong enough to challenge concerns about an immediate slowdown in AI demand, they did not resolve questions about the sustainability of AI spending, elevated bond yields, tighter US export restrictions or Nvidia’s future leadership, noted Chanana. “These concerns are particularly relevant for Singapore’s semiconductor companies, which are exposed to global capital spending cycles and have already experienced considerable share-price volatility.”

Nvidia’s eyewatering performance comes amid the huge scandal surrounding the company and its co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned following allegations of at least two extramarital affairs – one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with a company executive.

Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on the call that the company’s board has no intention to reinstate Huang, despite petitions from both employees and industry leaders, and will continue to search for its next permanent chief.

Chanana said that Huang’s departure does not undermine Nvidia’s existing technology or demand overnight, but “it raises questions about whether the company can maintain the same pace of innovation and execution over time”.

“An internal appointment of a new CEO could offer greater continuity in customer relationships, engineering priorities and supplier coordination, while an external hire might bring fresh perspectives but also greater uncertainty around execution.”

In particular, she noted that interim CEO Colette Kress, who has been the company’s chief financial officer for 13 years, delivered a “reassuring” performance on the earnings call, emphasising strategic continuity and the company’s ability to execute its technology roadmap without Huang, whose vision and supply-chain relationships were vital to Nvidia’s success thus far.

As the US authorities investigate whether Singapore company Megaspeed International was involved in smuggling Nvidia chips to China, Nvidia also stopped disclosing the scale of its business in Singapore since 2025, according to a report by the Financial Times (FT) on Nov 17.

Singapore primarily serves as the company’s global hub, and only a small quantity of its chips ends up in or goes through the Republic.

Before the 2025 reporting change, Nvidia said in its financial filing that it booked sales based on the billing locations of its customers, but the end-customer’s location “may be different than our customer’s billing location”.

It added that “most shipments associated with Singapore revenue were to locations other than Singapore, and shipments to Singapore were insignificant”, according to the filings.

According to FT’s report, the Republic was the company’s second-biggest geographic area by revenue in January 2025, with the Singapore office generating US$23.7 billion in revenue, behind only the US and representing 18% of global income, based on customer billing location.

As at July 2025, around the time that Nvidia said it was cutting ties with Megaspeed, the company reported that the Singapore office accounted for 22% of total revenue.

In 2025, Nvidia switched from reporting geographic sales based on a customer’s billing address to the customer’s headquarters.

Its Singapore subsidiary accounted for US$104 billion of revenue in the 2025 calendar year, almost half of its worldwide revenue, and was 72% higher than a year ago.

According to FT, the Singapore subsidiary booked US$117.8 billion of revenue in the financial year ended January 2026, including US$13.6 billion of sales to another Nvidia company. But it generated just US$53 million in profit.

data.title: S’pore unveils AI missions to fight financial crime, improve SME financing, enable safe AI payments
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Singapore is launching three national artificial intelligence initiatives to combat financial crime, improve financing for smaller businesses, and enable AI agents to make transactions safely on behalf of users.

Speaking at the Singapore FinTech Festival at Singapore Expo on Nov 18, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said these missions will bring together financial institutions, technology companies, researchers and public agencies to build shared capabilities in a bid to achieve more than any institution could alone.

Singapore will also test promising solutions against global best practices and standards, and take those that work well towards wider deployment.

To strengthen the country’s ability to detect and disrupt financial crime, Gan, who is also chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), said the Republic must connect information across the financial system while strengthening detection within each institution.

“Scams are not confined within the boundary of one bank. A victim’s money can pass through several institutions within minutes. We will not be able to mitigate the risk if each institution sees only its part of the transaction chain,” he added.

He noted that a proof of value is already under way with five banks, pooling transaction data securely to allow AI models to find patterns that no single bank can see on its own.

The MAS will begin a design study in early 2027 to develop the blueprint, including its governance and operating model, he added.

Singapore also wants to help businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), gain better access to financing through richer data.

Using these data sets, AI can identify information and patterns that traditional approaches may miss, giving lenders a fuller picture of a firm’s creditworthiness, said Gan.

It will also support faster, better-informed lending decisions, make it easier to serve smaller businesses and lower the cost of borrowing for lenders.

Singapore will invite AI tech companies to develop and test solutions using realistic synthetic data, said Gan. These trials will assess whether AI and richer data can make SME financing more forward-looking and accessible before determining the longer-term data and infrastructure needed to scale them up.

The Republic will also look into enabling AI agents to make transactions safely on behalf of users.

While AI agents make cash management more efficient and speed up payments, they must operate within defined authority and limits, and institutions and enterprises remain accountable for actions taken on their behalf, with safeguards built in from the start, he said.

Singapore will work with the industry to test practical applications in controlled environments – such as embedding conditions into transactions – and examine the safeguards needed for wider use, including common approaches to identity, authority, accountability and interoperability.

“We want to establish Singapore as a leading AI innovation centre, with the policies, standards and infrastructure to support trusted use of AI agents in finance.”

Gan also unveiled the latest report for PayNow Generation 2, which sets out how Singapore will make payments simpler, safer and more accessible for all users.

This includes a new SGQR+ switch, which will enable Singapore residents and tourists to pay with any SGQR+ label using their preferred QR app, as well as other enhancements.

Gan also touched on the new US rules requiring companies to have licences to export or re-export advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore.

He said the Republic will act against those who do not abide by its laws, amid growing scrutiny of the possible diversion of advanced US AI chips to China.

“We value our international reputation, and we do not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate the laws of other countries in their international business activities,” he said. “We will act against those who flout our laws.”

In a separate fireside chat, Gan noted that ASEAN countries have varying levels of digital and AI readiness, with some at the forefront of technological development while others are at the start of their digitalisation journey.

The ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, signed in Manila on Nov 14, allows all 11 member states to agree on a set of provisions and interoperability standards, he said.

As the ASEAN chair for 2027, Singapore is already exploring initiatives under the agreement that can benefit member states, and discussions with members are ongoing to identify collaborative initiatives, said Gan.

When asked how Singapore could become a leading hub for building, testing and scaling AI applications, he highlighted the importance of continuing to build trust in AI.

Gan stressed the importance of building a conducive ecosystem to attract, develop and retain AI talent, both locally and internationally.

This includes encouraging Singaporeans to pursue careers in AI, keeping Singapore open to global talent, and fostering collaboration among AI talent through initiatives such as Kampong AI.

He also highlighted the need for continuous skills upgrading and training to ensure Singapore’s workforce remains equipped and ready for an AI-driven future.

data.title: New US AI, data centre curbs could slow down AI adoption, investment across South-east Asia
data.description:
SINGAPORE – The scandal surrounding former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang now risks escalating into the start of a war between the world’s two largest economies for a strategic resource: computing power.

The US’ move to curb both indirect AI chip shipments to China and its access to overseas data centres – ahead of a summit between the nations’ presidents – could be the first shot in the much-dreaded fragmentation of the global tech ecosystem.

If mounting US-China friction on tech dominance raises the cost of or limits access to AI models and computational capacity, it could slow down the global adoption of artificial intelligence needed for extracting broader economic value from the technology, said analysts.

The new measures, which will come into effect 90 days after it is gazetted in the US’ Federal Register, expand US chip export controls to cover Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, aiming to close routes through which smuggled chips have been reaching China. Licences are now required to export advanced chips to any non-US headquartered firms in these countries.

The measures also ban Chinese chip designers from using foreign chip foundries, such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company or South Korea’s Samsung, to manufacture chips.

Data centres in third countries are now required to obtain a US licence before supplying significant amounts of AI computing power to Chinese-owned or Chinese-headquartered firms.

The US goal is to crack down on companies such as Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and built data centres throughout South-east Asia.

Megaspeed came into the public eye on Nov 8 after the disclosure of an extramarital affair between Jensen Huang, co-founder of US chipmaker Nvidia, and Megaspeed’s former top executive Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who is suspected by the US of being a Chinese spy.

He stepped down as Nvidia chief executive officer on Nov 12, while she has been banned from re-entering Singapore and is believed to be in China.

Beyond the impact on China, the US restrictions on access to computing power may affect data centre investment across South-east Asia, including Singapore, which has an estimated 1.6GW of capacity spread across more than 70 facilities.

Most analysts believe Malaysia stands to lose the most, given that it has been the biggest beneficiary of the region’s data centre build-out.

However, the whole region will still suffer because restrictions on access to overseas cloud facilities would undermine the commercial case for expanding capacity to serve Chinese customers.

This could weigh on investment in data centres by both Chinese and US companies. Any resulting slowdown in investment would add to the drag from an anticipated cooling in the global AI export cycle in 2027.

Lim Siew Khee, an analyst at brokerage firm CGS International, expects the near-term impact on ASEAN markets to be felt mainly through slower AI-related capital expenditure and investment into 2027, particularly in Malaysia and Thailand, as investors await licensing clarity. 

However, enterprise cloud, sovereign AI and domestic digitalisation should sustain broader data centre investment.

Analysts said these new regulations were clearly rushed through, given that there were several drafting errors in the official document, and loopholes remained. For example, Chinese companies can still lease data centres in the US. However, American hyperscalers are unlikely to take any risks by providing access to Chinese companies, especially those that are direct competitors.

Swiss private bank Julius Baer analyst Enrico Chinello said compute – the hardware and the supporting infrastructure used to train AI models and run them – is increasingly being treated as a strategic resource, and access to it is becoming a point of mounting geopolitical friction.

“The AI market could be fragmenting into a US-aligned ecosystem and a Chinese one, each building its own chips, models and infrastructure,” he said.

London-based research and consultancy firm Capital Economics expects US chip restrictions to tighten further. Its senior China economist Leah Fahy said the US Congress looked set to include a series of even harsher chip restrictions in the National Defence Act, due to be passed in December.

“They include legislation that would strengthen congressional oversight of advanced chip exports, mandate chip-tracking, further restrict China’s remote access to US tech, and tighten controls on third-country exports of chipmaking equipment to China,” she said in a research report.

Come January, the Democratic Party, with a majority in both chambers of Congress, may choose to further intensify the push for a tougher approach on China and its access – both direct and indirect – to US tech.

Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Danish investment bank Saxo, said AI model developers in China are increasingly concerned that Washington could restrict their open-source and open-weight AI models on national security grounds.

“This matters because lower-cost Chinese models have gained international users, including American businesses,” she said.

Hence, if such restrictions materialise, they could limit global adoption of Chinese AI models, which are seen as quite capable and yet less expensive than US frontier models.

Chanana added: “This could raise AI adoption costs for businesses globally, including American companies increasingly using cheaper Chinese models for coding, automation and routine tasks.”

This could result in a slowdown of the next phase of AI’s economic value creation.

“As the AI investment cycle shifts from building infrastructure towards adoption, affordable models are crucial for businesses to scale AI applications and generate measurable productivity gains,” Chanana said.

Accelerated fragmentation, with separate US and Chinese technology ecosystems, could potentially reduce competition, efficiency and innovation.
